title: The Economics of Work and Technology (Gresham College, The Future of Work series, Lecture 2)
author: Daniel Susskind

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Automation education: Adaptability helps but cannot suffice
st.an: The source supports the claim that education alone is insufficient by showing that the skill-biased framework cannot explain adverse outcomes for middle- and lower-skilled workers. It materially develops the proposition through task-level analysis and the distinction between technological substitution and complementarity, though it does not address geography, occupational identity or technology-sector power.
qs: Uh, and it turns out, as we're going to see, that skill bias view of technological change, which focuses entirely on high-skilled workers and lowskilled workers, doesn't really have us anything interesting to tell us about what's going on in the middle of the labor market.

Uh it's going to turn out that thinking about the world of work in terms of individual tasks rather than entire jobs is going to be a very revealing way of thinking about the impact of technology on work.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that technology generally transforms and reallocates tasks rather than eliminating whole occupations, and it distinguishes task-level substitution from complementarity. Its radiology example reinforces productivity-enhancing augmentation and work redesign, while its concern that more capable AI could eventually strengthen substitution remains explicitly tentative. It does not materially address legal verification, user expertise or operating-model implementation.
qs: Uh it's actually evidence again that the the the more interesting and important changes are taking place deeper down, lower down, at the level of the underlying tasks rather than at the level of job titles.

But if you look at uh the the evidence in practice actually it turns out that in many cases these uh systems are simply making radiologists more productive directly complementing them at the work that they do.

kp.k: Tasks, not job titles, reveal automation's effects
kp.d: Susskind argues that occupations—including lawyers, doctors, teachers and accountants—comprise multiple tasks rather than indivisible activities. Technology can displace workers from particular tasks while making others more valuable, so questions about entire occupations disappearing obscure important changes. He reports the argument that only elevator operators disappeared among 271 occupations in the 1950 US census over seven decades, but rejects occupational persistence as sufficient reassurance about automation. This is a general analytical framework, not a finding about legal employment.
qs: the really interesting things that are happening in the world of work are happening well below the level of jobs, they're happening in the individual tasks and activities that we do.

What it does is in a far more subtle way, it might displace us from performing particular tasks, but it can also at the same time make other tasks and other activities more valuable and more important for people to do.

kp.k: Employment depends on substitution and complementary demand
kp.d: Susskind distinguishes technology's substituting effect, which reduces demand for people to perform specific tasks, from its complementing effect, which increases demand for people to perform unautomated tasks. He presents their balance as the central explanation of technology's employment effects, rather than treating technical capability as a direct predictor of job losses.
qs: a machine substitutes for a human being when it displaces us from performing a particular task or activity and reduces the demand for us to perform that task.
They can also increase the demand for human beings to do tasks that haven't yet been automated.
the effect of technology on work depends upon the balance between these two rival forces.

kp.k: Productivity can expand demand for remaining human tasks
kp.d: The first complementary mechanism is direct productivity improvement in tasks that remain human. Susskind illustrates this with power looms, spinning machinery, drivers using satellite navigation and accountants using computational software. The demand-expansion mechanism is conditional: productivity gains must translate into lower prices or better products and services for consumers.
qs: new technologies, even if they displace some workers from certain tasks, they can often make workers more productive at unautomated tasks.

And if those productivity increases are then passed on to consumers in the form of lower prices or better quality products and services, you're going to see more demand for the work of human beings to do those tasks.
Or think of an accountant who uses Excel or other computational software to do harder, more intractable tax calculations.

kp.k: Economic growth indirectly increases demand for human work
kp.d: Susskind's 'bigger pie' mechanism links technological productivity growth to rising incomes, greater demand for goods and services, and additional demand for unautomated tasks. He reports global GDP per head rising from a few hundred for most of history to approximately $12,000 today. For 1700–2000, he cites aggregate economic growth of 113fold in the UK, 171fold in Japan, 1,699fold in Brazil, 2,300fold in Australia and 15,241fold in the US, attributing the long-run expansion essentially to technological progress.
qs: as productivity increases incomes rise demand for goods and services grows and so demand is going to grow for workers to perform tasks that haven't been automated to produce those goods and services.
Today, global GDP per head is something like $12,000.
the Japanese economy grew 171fold, the Brazilian economy 1,699fold, the Australian 2,300fold, the US economy a whopping 15,241fold.

kp.k: Changing consumption creates new, difficult-to-predict human tasks
kp.d: The 'changing pie' mechanism concerns changing expenditure patterns and new industries, not merely larger output. Susskind describes historical movement from farms to factories to offices, where displaced workers could find unautomated tasks. He uses the NHS, search-engine optimization, social-media management and prompt-related work to argue that future activities can be difficult or impossible to anticipate because their underlying technologies and concepts do not yet exist.
qs: New industries are created, new tasks have to be done that haven't been automated. And that means more demand for human beings.
people displaced from farms could tumble into factories. People displaced from factories could tumble into offices. Each time they could find new tasks to do that hadn't yet been automated.
It's not simply that these sorts of activities were hard to imagine. They were, you know, impossible to imagine.

kp.k: Radiology illustrates technical success without predicted employment collapse
kp.d: Susskind reports Hinton's 2016 recommendation to stop training radiologists because deep learning would outperform them within five years. He contrasts this with a 2018 algorithm tested on 14 diseases: it matched radiologists on 10, underperformed on three and outperformed on one. Despite expanding AI-enabled radiology devices, the US employment chart he presents shows rising filled positions. Susskind attributes this to productivity improvements, demand for medical services and redistribution of radiologists' tasks. He also reports Hinton's 2025 clarification that he meant image analysis and had been wrong about timing, not direction. The lecture supplies no sample size or precise employment-chart endpoint.
qs: So in 2018, scientists trained an algorithm to detect 14 different diseases um in a matter of seconds.
So for 10 of these diseases, the algorithm performed just as well as radiologists. For three of them, it underperformed compared with radiologists. And for one, uh the algorithm outdid the experts.
Hinton was right about the technology, but he was completely wrong about the economic impact on work.
He didn't make clear that he was speaking purely about image analysis and was wrong on timing but not the direction he added.

kp.k: ATMs displaced cash handling while teller employment increased
kp.d: Susskind reports that US teller employment more than doubled in the chart beginning in 1970 while ATM deployment rose. His explanation is that ATMs freed tellers for face-to-face support and financial guidance, improved services and reduced branch operating costs. He presents rising incomes and changing preferences toward relationship banking as possible additional indirect mechanisms, rather than separately demonstrated causal estimates. The transcript does not specify the chart's endpoint.
qs: if you look at the story of tellers and ATMs in the United States since 1970 that bottom line ATMs soaring and employment as bank tellers rising as well more than doubling in fact according uh to this chart.
ATMs didn't make tellers more productive at handing out cash, but they did free them up to focus on other activities like offering face-to-face support or providing financial guidance.
ATMs also helped reduce the cost of running branches

kp.k: Skill-biased technological change shaped education policy
kp.d: Susskind characterizes the late-twentieth-century mainstream account as a benign view in which technology benefits all workers but benefits skilled workers more. He connects computer diffusion and increasing capability to greater demand for educated workers and a rising college-to-high-school wage premium. He argues that this account encouraged education expansion, citing Clinton's 1996 ambition to universalize the 13th and 14th years of education, Blair's university-participation ambition and Obama's 2010 emphasis on postsecondary education and training. These are reported policy positions, not evidence that education necessarily resolves future AI displacement.
qs: Technology is going to benefit all workers, but it's going to benefit some workers, these skilled workers, more than others.
this skillbiased view of technological change really shapes how politicians and policymakers think about how to respond to the impact of technology on work.
There's a sort of metaphorical race going on between people and machines. You have to provide more education so people can keep up.

kp.k: Polarization and wage declines challenged the benign account
kp.d: Susskind identifies two empirical problems for his characterization of skill-biased technological change. Starting at some point in the 1980s, many economies experienced employment polarization: low- and high-skilled occupations expanded while middle-skilled occupations contracted. Separately, US charts show real wage declines among lower-skilled workers from the 1980s to a loosely specified recent period, alongside increases for higher-skilled workers. He argues that these absolute losses and middle-market changes required a framework beyond a simple high-versus-low skill premium.
qs: It's a phenomenon known as polarization or hollowing out.
It means there's more high paid professionals and managers.
what's going on at the lower end of the labor market is actually far from benign.
you're seeing a decline in the real wages of those lowskilled workers.

kp.k: Historical economists also anticipated technological unemployment
kp.d: Susskind presents concern about technology-induced displacement as an exception within economic thought rather than an entirely new position. He recounts Ricardo's reversal in the 1821 edition of his work after its 1817 publication, Keynes's 1930 account of labor-saving innovation outrunning new uses for labor, and Leontief's early-1980s analogy between displaced horses and potentially displaced humans. These are historical views reported by Susskind, not present-day employment forecasts established by the lecture.
qs: his lifelong assumption that machines would be a quote general good for labor was he said quote a mistake.
This means unemployment due to our discovery of means of economizing the use of labor through new technologies outrunning the pace at which we can find new uses for labor.
what uh the combustion engine did to horses robots and computers would eventually do to us.

kp.k: Historical complementarity prevailed despite disruption and dislocation
kp.d: Susskind argues that complementary demand historically outweighed task substitution, explaining why technological progress did not produce the persistent mass unemployment repeatedly feared. He cites British unemployment hovering around 5% up to 1900 despite Industrial Revolution machinery and resistance. He calls the broader period an 'age of labor', while acknowledging substantial disruption, differences across times and places, and a history more nuanced than his general account. His broad employment conclusion is the lecture's interpretation, not a detailed causal demonstration.
qs: up until 1900 in spite of all this technological progress during the industrial revolution there's no signs of large pools of unemployed people.
Technological progress has brought with it huge disruptions and dislocations.
Up until now, in the battle between this harmful substituting force and this helpful complimenting force, the latter has won out.
The story's uh never been, you know, quite as clear as this at different times and in different places

kp.k: AI task encroachment may overturn historical employment resilience
kp.d: Susskind closes with tentative questions rather than a settled displacement forecast. He describes machines encroaching on physical, cognitive and emotional tasks, with ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini representing a recent chapter in a longer technological trajectory. He asks whether expanding capabilities strengthen substitution while weakening complementarity by shrinking the set of unautomated tasks. Generative AI's reach into white-collar activities raises the question of where displaced workers could move next; he explicitly reserves fuller examination for later lectures.
qs: I call this process a process of task encroachment just this gradual but relentless encroachment in our working lives of these technologies.
whether or not the substituting force might be growing in strength given the technological changes that are taking place.
we are being forced to retreat to a shrinking set of tasks and activities that these machines these technologies cannot yet do.
Where in the economy are there going to be all these unautomated tasks that will provide a refuge for human workers as they might have provided in the past when technology was far less capable.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Susskind argues that automation changes tasks within jobs rather than necessarily eliminating whole occupations; its employment effects depend on the balance between substitution and complementarity.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain lecture about work and technology, not a forecast specifically about legal markets. Susskind includes lawyers among professions whose jobs comprise multiple activities. His central claim is that technology can reduce demand for humans in particular tasks while increasing demand in others. He identifies three complementary mechanisms: greater productivity in remaining human tasks, economy-wide growth that increases demand, and changing consumption and new industries that create unautomated tasks. He presents these mechanisms as explaining why past automation has not produced persistent aggregate technological unemployment, while acknowledging disruption and dislocation.

pts.k: Susskind claims that AI's success at medical image analysis has coexisted with increased radiologist employment because task automation can also complement practitioners.
pts.d: Susskind distinguishes technical capability from its economic consequences. He says medical AI can match or exceed specialists on some diagnostic tasks, but US radiologist employment has nevertheless increased. He explains this through direct productivity gains, increased demand for medical services as incomes grow, and practitioners shifting time toward other valuable hospital tasks. Hinton's 2016 recommendation to stop training radiologists is a prediction Susskind critiques, not Susskind's own recommendation.

pts.k: Susskind tentatively raises the possibility that increasingly capable AI will strengthen substitution and weaken the complementary forces that have historically sustained human employment.
pts.d: He describes a continuing process of 'task encroachment' across physical, cognitive and emotional activities, with generative AI representing a recent chapter rather than an entirely new process. He argues that the set of tasks machines cannot perform is shrinking and asks whether displaced workers will still find sufficient unautomated work. This is framed as an open question for future lectures, not a definite prediction of mass unemployment or a quantified forecast of job losses.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The medical-AI argument draws on reported diagnostic comparisons and charts of device growth and radiology positions; the transcript does not supply full study citations or chart data.
pts.d: Susskind cites a Stanford system, placed in 2017 by the lecture's chronology, that classified photographs of possible skin cancer as accurately as leading dermatologists. He describes a 2018 radiology algorithm tested on 14 diseases: matching radiologists on ten, underperforming on three and outperforming on one. He also refers to charts showing growth in AI-enabled radiology devices and US radiology positions filled. These are the offered basis for the coexistence of technical advances and employment growth. His explanation of the complementary mechanisms is qualitative; no numerical causal decomposition or radiologist productivity estimate is provided.

pts.k: Historical examples and economic reasoning support the task-based framework; the future-AI concern is an extrapolation rather than a measured employment forecast.
pts.d: Susskind invokes charts showing US bank-teller employment more than doubling alongside ATM adoption, British unemployment hovering around 5% during industrialisation up to 1900, and long-run economic growth. He uses the rise of healthcare, digital occupations and changing banking services to illustrate new demand and tasks. Labour-market polarisation and falling real wages for some low-skilled US workers motivate his move beyond a simple skill-biased account. He also invokes economist David Autor's argument about complementarities. For future AI, he points to growing capabilities, including ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, but supplies no benchmark, estimated displacement rate or model establishing when the historical balance will reverse.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Susskind separates a historical account extending to the 2025 lecture from a tentative concern about the rest of this century.
pts.d: The medical examples run from 2017–2018 to the lecture's present; the exact employment-chart period is not specified in the transcript. The broader historical claim covers industrialisation through the present. Complementarity depends on tasks remaining unautomated; the direct productivity mechanism also depends on gains reaching consumers through lower prices or better quality. His future question concerns whether these conditions persist as AI becomes more capable during this century, without a specific tipping-point date. Hinton's five-year forecast is discussed only as a contrasting prediction that failed to capture the economic outcome.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The relevant groups are workers across occupations, especially medical practitioners and white-collar workers, alongside consumers benefiting from productivity improvements.
pts.d: Radiologists and other medical practitioners can lose particular diagnostic tasks while becoming more productive and moving to other activities. White-collar workers are central to the prospective concern because generative AI can perform many office-work tasks that previously provided a destination for workers displaced from agriculture and manufacturing. Consumers may receive cheaper or better services, increasing demand for remaining human work. Historically, Susskind describes uneven effects across skill groups, including pressure on middle-skilled occupations and absolute real-wage declines for some low-skilled US workers. Lawyers appear as an example of task-bundled professional work; the lecture does not offer distinct claims about law-firm staffing, legal fees, clients or legal-service providers.
